points.guide: The magnetic field strength of an infinitely long current-carrying wire as given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ (and the direction of the field from the direction of the current).
aims: Determine the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire with the right-hand grip rule.
Calculate the field strength near a long straight wire using $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

slides.title: The field around a straight wire
bullets: The field lines are circles centred on the wire, in planes at right angles to it
Right-hand grip rule: thumb along the conventional current, and the fingers curl the way the field goes
Reverse the current and the field reverses
The field gets weaker further out, so the circles are drawn further apart
Seen end-on: a dot means current out of the page (an arrow coming towards you), a cross means into the page
slides.notes: A quick reminder of D.2: put plotting compasses round a vertical wire carrying a few amps and reverse the current. The guide expects students to find the field direction from the current direction.

slides.title: Circles round a wire
slides.alt: Left: a vertical wire with the current I upwards and two circular field lines round it, drawn in perspective; the field goes anticlockwise seen from above. Right: two end-on views. A dot means current out of the page, with the field circling anticlockwise. A cross means current into the page, with the field circling clockwise.
bullets: Current up the wire: the field circles anticlockwise, seen from above
Dot (current out of the page): anticlockwise
Cross (current into the page): clockwise
slides.notes: Check each view with the right-hand grip rule.

slides.title: Field strength near a long straight wire
bullets: $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ $\text{T m A}^{-1}$, the permeability of free space
Twice as far from the wire, half the field: $B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$
Strictly for an infinitely long wire: a good model when the distance is much smaller than the length of the wire
slides.notes: New for exams from 2028. The 2028 data booklet adds this equation. Point out that $\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi} = 2 \times 10^{-7}$ $\text{T m A}^{-1}$, which makes mental estimates quick.

slides.title: A lightning stroke
slides.question: A lightning stroke carries a peak current of 30 kA. Treating the stroke as a long straight vertical wire, find the magnetic field strength 100 m from it at that moment, and compare it with the Earth's field of about $5 \times 10^{-5}$ T.
slides.hint: Change kA to A first. The field falls off as $1/r$, and the $\pi$ in the equation cancels.

steps.text: Use the field of a long straight wire.
That is about the same as the Earth's field, but it lasts only a fraction of a millisecond.

slides.notes: New for exams from 2028. Lightning currents are typically tens of kiloamperes, so even 100 m away the brief magnetic pulse is as strong as the Earth's field.

slides.title: A compass beside a vertical wire
slides.question: A long vertical wire carries a current of 6.0 A upwards. A small compass sits on the bench 2.0 cm due east of the wire. Find (a) the direction and (b) the size of the magnetic field of the wire at the compass.
slides.hint: Point your right thumb up along the current and look at which way your fingers move as they pass the east side of the wire.

steps.text: (a) Seen from above, the field circles anticlockwise round a current coming up towards you.
On the east side of the wire, anticlockwise means pointing north.
The field at the compass, pointing north:

slides.notes: New for exams from 2028 (part b). Here the wire's field points the same way as the Earth's horizontal field, so the needle still points north. Ask where on the bench the compass would swing the most.

points.guide: The magnitude and direction of the force on a charge moving in a magnetic field as given by $F = qvB\sin\theta$, where $B$ is the magnetic field strength.
aims: Calculate the magnetic force on a moving charge using $F = qvB\sin\theta$.
Find the direction of the force, and explain why it leaves the kinetic energy unchanged.

slides.title: Magnetic forces need moving charges
bullets: A magnetic field exerts a force on a charge only while the charge is moving
A stationary charge, or one moving along the field lines, feels no magnetic force
The force is largest when the charge moves at right angles to the field
A current is moving charge, which is why a wire carrying a current feels a force too
slides.notes: A moving charge has a magnetic field of its own, which is one way of seeing why only moving charges are affected. Contrast with an electric field, which pushes on a charge whether or not it moves.

slides.title: The force on a moving charge
bullets: $\theta$: the angle between the velocity and the field
$B$: the magnetic field strength, in tesla (T)
A charge of 1 C moving at 1 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at right angles to a 1 T field feels a force of 1 N
slides.notes: In the data booklet. The last bullet gives students a feel for the tesla: 1 T is a strong field (a school magnet is a few tenths of a tesla at most).

slides.title: Which way is the force?
bullets: The force is at right angles to both the velocity and the field
Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger along the Field, seCond finger along the Current, thuMb gives the force (Motion)
The "current" is the direction a positive charge moves
For an electron, point the second finger opposite to its velocity
Field drawn as dots: out of the page; as crosses: into the page
slides.notes: The deck also shows a right-hand rule (fingers curl from v towards B, thumb gives the force on a positive charge). It gives the same answer: let students choose one rule and use it every time. The topic page uses Fleming's left-hand rule.

slides.title: Fleming's left-hand rule
slides.alt: A left hand with the thumb pointing up, labelled F, the first finger pointing forwards and to the right, labelled B, and the second finger pointing down and to the right, labelled I. The three are at right angles to each other.
bullets: First finger: the Field, $B$
Second finger: the current, $I$ (the way a positive charge moves)
Thumb: the force, or motion, $F$
slides.notes: The three directions must be at right angles. For an electron, point the second finger opposite to its velocity.

slides.title: No work done, no change of speed
bullets: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity
So it does no work on the particle: $W = Fs\cos 90^{\circ} = 0$
The speed and the kinetic energy stay constant; only the direction of motion changes
An electric field, by contrast, can speed a charge up or slow it down
slides.notes: The guide's guidance asks for this point specifically: in a magnetic field alone, a charged particle's kinetic energy never changes. It is a common exam explanation.

slides.title: An alpha particle in a field
slides.question: An alpha particle (charge $+2e$) moves at $1.5 \times 10^{7}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of 40° to a uniform magnetic field of 0.60 T. Find the size of the magnetic force on it.
slides.hint: Use the angle between the velocity and the field, and remember that an alpha particle carries two elementary charges.

steps.text: The charge of the alpha particle:
Multiply by the sine of the angle.

slides.notes: Alpha particles from radioactive decay do move at around this speed. Ask: at what angle would the force be zero, and at what angle largest?

slides.title: Which way does the electron go?
slides.question: An electron moves due north through a region where the magnetic field points vertically downwards. In which direction is the magnetic force on it?
slides.hint: Find the direction of the conventional current first: an electron moving north counts as a current flowing south.

steps.text: The electron is negative, so the conventional current is to the south.
Left hand: first finger down (field), second finger south (current).
The thumb points east: the force on the electron is due east.

slides.notes: A positive charge moving north in the same field would be pushed west. Students who forget to reverse for the electron get exactly that answer.

points.guide: The motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field (including the determination of the charge-to-mass ratio from its path).
aims: Explain why a charged particle moving at right angles to a uniform magnetic field follows a circle, and derive $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.
Determine the charge-to-mass ratio of a particle from the radius of its path.

slides.title: Why the path is a circle
bullets: Moving at right angles to a uniform field, the particle feels a force $qvB$ of constant size
The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes only the direction
A force of constant size, always at right angles to the motion, gives uniform circular motion (A.2)
The magnetic force is the centripetal force
Positive and negative particles curve in opposite directions
slides.notes: Be careful with the wording: the size of the force is constant, but its direction keeps turning so that it always points to the centre.

slides.title: Circling in a magnetic field
bullets: Ask: which way round would a negative particle go?
Ask: what would happen to the circle if the particle moved faster?

slides.title: Deriving the radius of the path
slides.start: A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ moves at speed $v$ at right angles to a uniform field $B$, so $\sin\theta = 1$.

steps.text: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force

slides.notes: This is not in the data booklet: students should be able to derive it every time.

slides.title: Deriving the time for one orbit
slides.start: Use the radius just found and the time to travel once round the circle.

steps.text: One orbit is a distance $2\pi r$ at speed $v$

slides.notes: A faster particle moves in a bigger circle but takes the same time to go round. This is the idea behind the cyclotron (not on the syllabus).

slides.title: Reading the circle
bullets: $r \propto mv$: faster or heavier particles make bigger circles
A bigger charge or a stronger field makes a tighter circle
The time for one orbit does not depend on the speed
A velocity component along the field is not affected, so the path becomes a helix
Charged particles from the Sun spiral along the Earth's field lines into the polar atmosphere, where they cause the aurora
slides.notes: The particles come mainly in the solar wind and in coronal mass ejections. They excite oxygen and nitrogen in the upper atmosphere, which then emit light: oxygen mostly green (and some red), nitrogen blue to violet.

slides.title: An electron in a weak field
slides.question: An electron moving at $4.0 \times 10^{6}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field of 2.5 mT at right angles to the field. Find (a) the radius of its path and (b) the time it takes to go once round.
slides.hint: Convert mT to T first. The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force; the time follows from the circumference and the speed.

steps.text: (a) Use the radius of the path.

slides.notes: Part (b) can also be done with $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$, without the radius: a good check.

slides.title: Measuring the charge-to-mass ratio
bullets: Rearranging $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$ gives $\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{v}{Br}$
So the radius of the path in a known field, and the speed, give the particle's charge-to-mass ratio
In a fine-beam tube, electrons accelerated through a p.d. $V$ move in a circle in the uniform field of a pair of coils; a little gas makes the path glow
Measure $V$, the field $B$ (set by the coil current) and the radius $r$
The ratio helps identify the particle: the electron's is about 1800 times the proton's
slides.notes: The guide requires this determination. If a fine-beam tube is available, show it in a darkened room and let students read the radius off the scale inside the bulb.

slides.title: Deriving e/m for the fine-beam tube
slides.start: Electrons start from rest, are accelerated through a p.d. $V$, then move in a circle of radius $r$ in a field $B$.

steps.text: Energy gained from the accelerating field
Speed from the radius of the circle

slides.notes: Because the radius is squared, its percentage uncertainty counts twice: measure it as carefully as possible (a diameter is easier to read than a radius).

slides.title: A fine-beam tube reading
slides.question: In a fine-beam tube, electrons accelerated from rest through 180 V move in a circle of diameter 10.0 cm in a uniform magnetic field of 0.90 mT. Find the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron.
slides.hint: Halve the diameter, and convert mT to T, before substituting into the equation just derived.

steps.text: Radius and field in SI units:
Use the result of the derivation.

slides.notes: The accepted value is $1.76 \times 10^{11}$ $\text{C kg}^{-1}$, so this is about 1% high. Ask which measurement most affects the result.

slides.title: A mass spectrometer
slides.alt: Positive ions with speed v enter a region of uniform magnetic field, directed out of the page, through a slit. They travel round a semicircle of radius r and hit a detector a distance x equal to 2r from the slit. A dashed, wider semicircle shows the path of heavier ions.
bullets: Positive ions enter at right angles to $B$ and go round half a circle
They land one diameter, $x = 2r$, from the entrance
Heavier ions, with the same charge and speed, follow a wider circle

slides.title: Deriving the mass in a mass spectrometer
slides.start: Ions of charge $q$ and speed $v$ enter a uniform field $B$ at right angles, travel round half a circle and hit a detector a distance $x$ from where they entered.

steps.text: The ions land one diameter away

slides.notes: Ions with the same charge and speed (given a single speed by a velocity selector) land at distances proportional to their masses, so the isotopes of an element separate.

slides.title: Identifying an isotope
slides.question: In a mass spectrometer, singly charged positive ions moving at $1.2 \times 10^{5}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ enter a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T at right angles. After half a circle they hit the detector 10.0 cm from the entrance. Find the mass of one ion in kg and in unified atomic mass units ($1\ \text{u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}$ kg).
slides.hint: The distance to the detector is the diameter of the circle, not its radius.

steps.text: Use the result of the derivation.

slides.notes: An ion of mass 20 u is neon-20, the commonest isotope of neon. Ions of neon-22 would land about 11 cm away.

points.guide: The magnitude and direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field as given by $F = BIL\sin\theta$.
aims: Derive and use $F = BIL\sin\theta$ for the force on a current-carrying conductor.
Find the direction of the force with Fleming's left-hand rule.

slides.title: The motor effect
bullets: A current is a flow of charge, so each moving charge in the wire feels a magnetic force
These forces add up to a force on the whole wire
No current, no force; reverse either the current or the field and the force reverses
The force is zero when the wire lies along the field, and largest at right angles to it
slides.notes: Demonstration: a strip of aluminium foil between the poles of a strong magnet jumps when a current passes through it. Reverse the current and it jumps the other way.

slides.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor
bullets: $\theta$: the angle between the wire (the current) and the field
$L$: the length of wire inside the field
Direction: Fleming's left-hand rule, with the second finger along the conventional current
slides.notes: In the data booklet. Note the order of the letters in the booklet (B I L), different from qvB.

slides.title: From moving charges to a force on a wire
slides.start: Charge $q$ flows along a length $L$ of wire in a time $t$, so it moves at speed $v = L/t$.

steps.text: Start from the force on a moving charge
Group the charge and the time
Current is charge per unit time, $I = q/t$

slides.notes: The same angle appears in both equations: the current flows in the direction the positive charges move.

slides.title: A wire between magnet poles
bullets: Ask: what happens if the current is reversed?
Ask: and if the magnet is turned round as well?

slides.title: A loudspeaker coil
slides.question: The coil of a loudspeaker sits in a radial magnetic field of 0.80 T, which is at right angles to the wire everywhere. The coil contains 4.5 m of wire. Find the force on the coil when the current in it is 0.50 A.
slides.hint: The field is perpendicular to every part of the wire, so use the whole length of wire in the field.

steps.text: The field is at right angles to the wire.

slides.notes: With an alternating current the force keeps reversing, so the coil and the cone attached to it vibrate and make sound.

slides.title: A power cable in the Earth's field
slides.question: A straight 100 m span of power cable runs north–south and carries a current of 250 A northwards. The Earth's field there is $5.0 \times 10^{-5}$ T, directed northwards and downwards at 60° to the horizontal. Find the size and direction of the force on the span.
slides.hint: The angle you need is the one between the current and the field. Only the part of the field at right angles to the cable produces a force.

steps.text: The angle between the current (north) and the field is 60°.
Direction: the downward part of the field and the northward current give, by the left-hand rule, a force to the west.

slides.notes: About 1 N on 100 m of heavy cable is negligible, but the method is the point. A cable running east–west would feel a force of 1.25 N, because then the whole field is at right angles to it.

points.guide: The force per unit length between parallel wires as given by $\dfrac{F}{L} = \mu_0\dfrac{I_1I_2}{2\pi r}$, where $r$ is the separation between the two wires.
aims: Derive and use $\dfrac{F}{L} = \mu_0\dfrac{I_1I_2}{2\pi r}$ for the force between parallel wires.
Explain why currents in the same direction attract, and why the forces on the two wires are equal.

slides.title: Two parallel currents
bullets: Each wire sits in the magnetic field of the other, so each feels a force
Currents in the same direction attract; in opposite directions they repel
Careful: this is the opposite of the rule for electric charges
The two forces are a Newton's third law pair: equal in size, even when the currents are different
slides.notes: Demonstration: two strips of aluminium foil hanging side by side, connected so that a large current from a low-voltage supply flows up one and down the other (they spring apart), then the same way in both (they pull together).

slides.title: Force between parallel wires
bullets: $\dfrac{F}{L}$: the force on each metre of either wire, in $\text{N m}^{-1}$
$r$: the separation of the wires
slides.notes: In the data booklet.

slides.title: Deriving the force per unit length
slides.start: Two long parallel wires a distance $r$ apart carry currents $I_1$ and $I_2$.

steps.text: The field of wire 1 at wire 2
This field is at right angles to wire 2, so the force on a length $L$ of wire 2 is

slides.notes: New for exams from 2028 (step 1 only): the field of a long straight wire is now in the guide and data booklet. The force between parallel wires was already on the syllabus. Starting from wire 2's field at wire 1 gives the same force, as Newton's third law requires.

slides.title: Using the parallel-wire equation
bullets: Ordinary currents give tiny forces: two 1 A wires 1 m apart feel $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N on each metre
This once defined the ampere; since 2019 the ampere has been defined by fixing the size of the elementary charge
Very large currents, such as in a short circuit, give forces big enough to make cables jump
Convert the separation to metres, and multiply the force per metre by the length when the total force is wanted
slides.notes: Some older resources still give the force between wires as the definition of the ampere: it was replaced in the 2019 redefinition of the SI units.

slides.title: Currents in the same direction
bullets: Use the grip rule to find the field of each wire at the other wire
Then use Fleming's left-hand rule for each force

slides.title: Jump leads
slides.question: While a car is being jump-started, its two jump leads lie side by side, 1.5 cm apart. Each carries a current of 150 A, in opposite directions. Find the force on each metre of lead, and say whether the leads attract or repel.
slides.hint: Both currents are 150 A. Remember to change the separation into metres.

steps.text: Use the force per unit length.
The currents are in opposite directions, so the leads repel.

slides.notes: Starter motors draw well over 100 A for a second or two, so the leads really do twitch apart.

slides.title: Finding the current
slides.question: Two straight parallel rods in a laboratory, each 2.0 m long and 3.0 cm apart, carry equal currents in the same direction. They attract each other with a force of $4.0 \times 10^{-3}$ N. Find the current in each rod.
slides.hint: Find the force per metre first, then put $I_1 = I_2 = I$ and rearrange for $I^{2}$.
slides.notes: The rods are 2.0 m long and only 3.0 cm apart, so treating them as infinitely long is reasonable.

points.guide: The motion of a charged particle in a uniform electric field.
aims: Describe the motion of a charged particle in a uniform electric field, both along the field and entering it at right angles.
Calculate the speed of a particle accelerated from rest through a p.d. $V$, and its deflection between parallel plates.

slides.title: A charge in a uniform electric field
bullets: Between parallel plates the field is uniform, so the force $F = qE$ is constant
Positive charges are pushed along the field; negative charges the opposite way
A constant force gives a constant acceleration, $\dfrac{qE}{m}$, so the equations of motion (A.1) apply
The field does work on the charge, so it can change its speed and kinetic energy
The weight of a particle such as an electron is negligible by comparison
slides.notes: For an electron in a field of $10^{4}$ $\text{V m}^{-1}$, the electric force is about $10^{-15}$ N and the weight about $10^{-29}$ N.

slides.title: Electric field equations (D.2)
bullets: Both are in the data booklet, under D.2
$V$: the p.d. between the plates; $d$: their separation

slides.title: Speed after accelerating from rest
slides.start: A particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ starts at rest and is accelerated through a p.d. $V$.

steps.text: Work done on the particle by the field
All of it becomes kinetic energy

slides.notes: This works only well below the speed of light. For electrons, keep accelerating p.d.s below a few kilovolts in questions.

slides.title: Why the path between the plates is a parabola
slides.start: A particle enters the field at right angles to it with speed $u$. The field gives it an acceleration $a$ across the plates.

steps.text: Along the plates there is no force: constant velocity
Across the plates: uniform acceleration from rest
Since $y \propto x^{2}$, the path is a parabola, like a ball thrown horizontally

slides.notes: Compare with projectile motion in A.1: the electric force across the plates plays the part of gravity.

slides.title: Solving deflection problems
bullets: Split the motion into two directions at right angles, as for a projectile
Along the plates: constant speed, so the time in the field is the plate length divided by $u$
Across the plates: acceleration $\dfrac{qE}{m}$, starting from zero velocity
After leaving the plates: no force, so a straight line
Check the deflection is less than the gap: otherwise the particle hits a plate

slides.title: Deflection between parallel plates
bullets: Ask: how would the path of a proton at the same speed differ?
Ask: what happens to the path if the p.d. is doubled?

slides.title: Accelerating protons
slides.question: In a small accelerator, protons start from rest and are accelerated through a potential difference of 5.0 kV. Find their final speed. ($m_p = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}$ kg)
slides.hint: The work done by the field becomes the protons' kinetic energy.
slides.notes: An electron through the same p.d. would be about 43 times faster (the square root of the mass ratio, 1836).

slides.title: An oscilloscope beam
slides.question: In an oscilloscope tube, electrons moving at $3.0 \times 10^{7}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ pass between two parallel plates 4.0 cm long and 2.0 cm apart, entering at right angles to the field. The p.d. between the plates is 150 V. Find (a) the electric field strength, (b) the time the electrons spend between the plates and (c) how far they are deflected sideways.
slides.hint: The speed along the plates sets the time in the field. Across the plates the electrons start with zero velocity and accelerate steadily.
slides.notes: The deflection (1.2 mm) is well under half the gap, so the electrons get through. On the screen, some distance beyond the plates, the spot moves much further because the beam leaves at an angle.

points.guide: The motion of a charged particle in perpendicularly orientated uniform electric and magnetic fields.
aims: Explain how perpendicular electric and magnetic fields can let a charged particle pass through undeflected.
Derive and use $v = \dfrac{E}{B}$ for a velocity selector.

slides.title: Crossed electric and magnetic fields
bullets: Set up the electric field, the magnetic field and the velocity all at right angles to each other
The electric force $qE$ doesn't depend on the speed; the magnetic force $qvB$ does
With the fields the right way round, the two forces point in opposite directions
If they are equal, the net force is zero: the particle goes straight through at constant speed
slides.notes: Use the left-hand rule to check that the forces oppose in the arrangement on the board before doing any calculation.

slides.title: Deriving the selected speed
slides.start: For a particle that passes through undeflected, the electric and magnetic forces are equal and opposite.

steps.text: The charge and the mass have gone: any particle with this speed passes straight through

slides.title: Faster, slower, other particles
bullets: Slower particles: the magnetic force is too small, so they are pushed in the direction of the electric force
Faster particles: the magnetic force wins
A negative particle at the same speed also passes: both forces reverse together
Used to give ions a single speed before they enter a mass spectrometer

slides.title: A velocity selector
bullets: Ask: which way would a slower particle be deflected?

slides.title: Setting up a velocity selector
slides.question: Two parallel plates 8.0 mm apart have a p.d. of 1200 V between them, and a uniform magnetic field of 0.30 T acts at right angles to the electric field. Find (a) the speed of the ions that pass straight through and (b) what happens to electrons moving at the same speed.
slides.hint: Find the electric field strength from the plates first. For (b), think about what happens to each force when the sign of the charge changes.

steps.text: (b) Both forces reverse but stay equal, so the electrons also pass straight through.
